items.title: Conditional-kernel tail and atom evaluations are measurable
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define
$$a(s,t):=K(s,(t,\infty)),\qquad b(s,t):=K(s,\{t\}).$$
Both maps are $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable. If $S_0$ and $T_0$ are measurable random elements of $S$ and $\mathbb R$ on one probability space, and $U$ is any measurable real random variable on that space, then $a(S_0,T_0)$, $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)$, and $a(S_0,T_0)+U b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable. The middle expression equals $K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$.
items.strategy: Lift K to the product base S×R, prove the strict-order and equality relation indicators are product-measurable, and apply measurable integration against a kernel. Then use product measurability and continuous arithmetic maps for the displayed p-values.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.3, PDF pp. 33–35
A. J. Brockwell, Universal Residuals: A Multivariate Transformation, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1

items.title: Randomizing across CDF jumps gives a uniform variable
items.statement:
Let $Y$ be a real random variable with cumulative distribution function $F(y)=P(Y\le y)$, and let $U$ be independent of $Y$ with the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$. Write $F(y-):=P(Y<y)$ and $\Delta F(y):=F(y)-F(y-)=P(Y=y)$. Then
$$V:=F(Y-)+U\Delta F(Y)$$
has the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, for arbitrary continuous, discrete, mixed, or singular laws of $Y$.
items.strategy: Use the generalized quantile q=inf{x:F(x)≥u}. The mass below q contributes F(q−), the jump at q contributes the remaining u−F(q−), and the region above q contributes zero; handle flat CDF intervals and the endpoints explicitly.

references.title: A. J. Brockwell, Universal Residuals: A Multivariate Transformation, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1

items.title: Finite-group randomization setups
items.statement: A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

references.title: Peter B. Stark, Statistics 240 Lecture Notes, Part 8: Resampling Methods, §1.3, PDF pp. 10–11
Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3

items.title: Tied upper ranks on a finite multiset
items.statement:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.
items.strategy: Sort distinct values into tie blocks. A block of size r_j occurs with probability r_j/m, and its randomized rank is uniform on the consecutive interval of length r_j/m assigned to that block. The inclusive rank is the interval's right endpoint.

references.title: Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, randomized p-value result

items.title: Randomized conditional upper-tail p-values
items.statement:
Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

references.title: A. J. Brockwell, Universal Residuals: A Multivariate Transformation, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1
George Deligiannidis, Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, PDF pp. 77–78

items.title: Orbit upper-tail rank p-values
items.statement:
For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

references.title: Peter B. Stark, Statistics 240 Lecture Notes, Part 8: Resampling Methods, §1.3, PDF pp. 10–11
Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3

items.title: Randomized conditional p-values are uniform
items.statement:
Under the simple null and the supplied conditional law in [[def-randomized-conditional-p-value]], for every $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_0(p_U\le u\mid\sigma(S))=u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},$$
while the nonrandomized upper-tail value satisfies
$$P_0(p_0\le u\mid\sigma(S))\le u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely}.$$
Thus the randomized value is conditionally uniform and the inclusive-tail value is conditionally superuniform, including when the conditional law has atoms.
items.strategy: Apply the randomized probability integral transform to each conditional law. The nonrandomized inclusive tail is the upper endpoint of the randomized interval and is therefore superuniform.

references.title: A. J. Brockwell, Universal Residuals: A Multivariate Transformation, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1
Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3 and randomized p-value result

items.title: Finite-group orbit-rank validity
items.statement: In a finite-group randomization setup, fix a null law invariant under the group action. Conditional on every orbit $O$ with positive probability, the data are uniform on the distinct points of $O$. For the orbit ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]], the inclusive p-value $p_0$ is superuniform under the null, and the independent-uniform tie-randomized value $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on each positive-probability orbit. Consequently, $p_U$ is also Uniform$(0,1)$ unconditionally.
items.strategy: First prove equal mass on distinct orbit points and constant transformation multiplicity by the stabilizer fibers. Then sort the orbit statistic values into tie blocks: their randomized rank intervals partition [0,1], while each inclusive rank is the right endpoint of its block.

references.title: Peter B. Stark, Statistics 240 Lecture Notes, Part 8: Resampling Methods, §1.3, PDF pp. 10–11
Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3

items.title: Conditional tests given a statistic
items.statement: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.3, PDF pp. 33–35
George Deligiannidis, Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, PDF pp. 77–78
Berkeley Stat 210A Course Reader, Testing with Nuisance Parameters, Conditional testing section

items.title: Sufficiency makes the conditional rejection probability nuisance-free
items.statement:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal S,\mathscr S)$ be standard Borel spaces as in [[def-standard-borel-space]]. Fix Polish topologies realizing these specified Borel sigma-algebras, as the standard-Borel definition permits. Let $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint parameter subsets, and write $\{P_\eta:\eta\in\Theta_0\}$ for the null subfamily. Let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Suppose there is one probability kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ such that, for every $\eta\in\Theta_0$, $K(S,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full data $X$ given $\sigma(S)$ under $P_\eta$. This is the common-kernel premise of sufficiency for the null subfamily in [[def-sufficient-statistic]]. For any measurable $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, define
$$q(s):=\int_{\mathcal X}\varphi(x)K(s,dx).$$
Then $q$ is measurable and $q(S)$ is a version of the conditional rejection probability of $\varphi$ given $S$ under every $P_\eta$. The same function $q$ works for every nuisance value, with conditional-expectation identities interpreted almost surely under each corresponding law.
items.strategy: Unfold the common-kernel sufficiency hypothesis and apply the conditional-integration identity to the bounded test function under each null law. Keep the a.s. exceptional sets parameter-specific; no common support is assumed.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.3, PDF pp. 33–35
Berkeley Stat 210A Course Reader, Testing with Nuisance Parameters, Conditional testing section

items.title: Conditional level implies unconditional level
items.statement: Let $\varphi$ be a test for nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]], let $S$ be a statistic, and let $\alpha\in[0,1]$. If for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$ there is a conditional-expectation version $q_\theta=E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$ with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely, then $E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. Consequently, the test has size at most $\alpha$, where size is the supremum of its rejection expectation over the null family as in [[def-test-size-and-power]].
items.strategy: Integrate the conditional-expectation version over the whole sample space, then use monotonicity of expectation and take the supremum over null parameters.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, PDF pp. 77–78
Berkeley Stat 210A Course Reader, Testing with Nuisance Parameters, Conditional testing section

title: Conditional and Finite-Group Exact Inference — Examples

items.title: Without null invariance a group-rank p-value can be anti-conservative
items.statement: For every finite group action and every null law, the inclusive group-average upper-tail rank is superuniform, even when the null law is not invariant under the group.
items.strategy: Use the two-point space with the swapping group and statistic T(x)=x. Compute the orbit-rank p-value at each point and the probability of p≤1/2 under a null law concentrated mostly at the larger point.

references.title: Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3

items.title: A permutation orbit with tied ranks and nontrivial stabilizers
items.statement: Let $G=S_3$ permute the coordinates of $\Omega=\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subset\{0,1\}^3$, give the three points equal probability, take $T(x)=x_1$, and use an independent $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. Each point has a stabilizer of size two. The group-average inclusive ranks are $p_0(e_1)=1/3$ and $p_0(e_2)=p_0(e_3)=1$. The randomized values are $p_U(e_1)=U/3$ and $p_U(e_2)=p_U(e_3)=1/3+2U/3$, illustrating how tied ranks fill adjacent intervals even when each orbit point has multiple group preimages.
items.strategy: List the six permutations, count their images with multiplicity for each observed point, and verify the tie-block intervals and uniform mixture directly.

references.title: Peter B. Stark, Statistics 240 Lecture Notes, Part 8: Resampling Methods, §1.3, PDF pp. 10–11
Jesse Hemerik and Jelle Goeman, Exact testing with random permutations, Sections 2–3

items.title: Fisher's exact test from two Bernoulli samples
items.statement:
Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
$$Q(s,\{k\})=\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}}{\binom{N}{s}},\qquad \max(0,s-n_2)\le k\le\min(n_1,s),$$
and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.
items.strategy: Count binary sequences with s successes, group them by the number k in the first sample, and cancel the common null weight. Then enumerate the n1=n2=2, s=2 conditional support and verify the conservative and randomized tail ranks.

references.title: Berkeley Stat 210A Course Reader, Testing with Nuisance Parameters, Conditional testing section
George Deligiannidis, Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, PDF pp. 77–78
